What ten years of tide records say about the bay

By Ana Ruiz 12 October 2026 6 min read Coast and climate

Since March 2016, a group of volunteers has read the tide gauge in the port at six in the morning and six in the evening, every day of the year. Their sheets, now ten years of them, are the longest record of the sea in the bay that anyone has kept by hand, and the council will publish them as open data.

The records are at https://example.org/a-very-long-address/that-goes-on/and-on/tide-records-2016-2026.csv, in a file whose columns are level_cm and read_at.

How the readings were taken

Each reading is the height of the water against the gauge, to the nearest centimetre, with the time, the wind and the state of the sea.

  • 7,300 readings a year, two a day.
  • 41 volunteers over ten years.
    • Nine of them from the start.
  • Fewer than one reading in a hundred left out.
  1. Read the gauge.
  2. Write the height.
  • A stack, not a list with markers.
  • Its items keep their list role.

We did not set out to measure the climate.

We wanted to know when to take the boats out.
